ch3-introduction.code:
print("Hello, World!")
print("Welcome to Python programming.")
ch3-introduction.output:
Hello, World!
Welcome to Python programming.
ch3-introduction.explanation: Python runs the statements one after another. Each print() call displays a line of text on the screen.
Python can be used as a calculator. Note that the division operator / always gives a float result.

ch3-introduction.code:
# This is a comment
print("Comments are ignored by Python")
ch3-introduction.explanation: A line starting with # is a comment. Python ignores comments when running the program.

ch3-installation.code:
print("Python installed successfully!")
print("Ready to write your first program.")
ch3-installation.output:
Python installed successfully!
Ready to write your first program.
ch3-installation.explanation: Once Python is installed you can save code in a .py file and run it from the command prompt or an IDE.

ch3-installation.code:
# First command after installation
print(4 + 6)
print("Python works!")
ch3-installation.explanation: This small program confirms that your Python installation is working correctly.

ch3-working.explanation: The interpreter reads and executes each statement from top to bottom, in the order written.
Python first evaluates the expression 10 + 20 and then displays its result.
A print() call can show text and a computed value together, separated by a space by default.

ch3-hello-world.explanation: The classic first program. It simply prints a line of text to the screen.
When two strings are written separately, print() puts a space between them automatically.
The + operator joins (concatenates) two strings into one before it is printed.

ch4-character-set.explanation: Python programs are written using letters and digits. Strings let you print such character sets easily.
The Python character set also includes special symbols used in programs and in text output.

ch4-tokens.explanation: Literals are the smallest tokens that hold a fixed value: integers, floats, strings and booleans.
Identifiers are the names you give to variables. They must start with a letter or underscore.
Operators are tokens that tell Python to perform an action, such as arithmetic or comparison.
Punctuators such as [ ] , are symbols that help structure the code; here they build a list.

ch4-variables.explanation: A variable is created the moment you assign a value to it using the = operator.
The right-hand side is evaluated first, then stored back into the variable. So count becomes 2.
Python lets you assign values to several variables in a single statement.

ch4-variables.code:
a = 1
b = 2
a, b = b, a
print("a =", a)
print("b =", b)
ch4-variables.explanation: Multiple assignment makes it easy to swap the values of two variables without a third variable.

ch4-input-output.code:
name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello", name)
ch4-input-output.output:
Enter your name: Aditya
Hello Aditya
ch4-input-output.explanation: input() reads text typed by the user as a string. The text inside the brackets is the prompt shown.

ch4-input-output.code:
a = int(input("Enter first number: "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))
print("Sum is", a + b)
ch4-input-output.output:
Enter first number: 12
Enter second number: 8
Sum is 20
ch4-input-output.explanation: input() returns a string, so int() is used to convert it to a number before adding.

ch4-input-output.code:
price = float(input("Enter price: "))
print("Price with tax:", price + price * 0.05)
ch4-input-output.explanation: float() converts the typed text into a decimal number. A 5% tax is added to the price.

ch4-input-output.code:
print("apple", "banana", "cherry", sep=", ")
print("End of line", end=" | ")
print("continues here")
ch4-input-output.output:
apple, banana, cherry
End of line | continues here
ch4-input-output.explanation: sep changes the separator between values, and end changes what is printed at the end of the line.

ch4-input-output.code:
x = input("Type anything: ")
print("You typed:", x)
ch4-input-output.output:
Type anything: Python
You typed: Python
ch4-input-output.explanation: Whatever the user types is stored in the variable x and then printed back on the screen.

ch4-structure.explanation: A Python program is a sequence of statements, each written on its own line.
The indented line forms a block that belongs to the if statement. Indentation defines blocks in Python.

ch4-structure.code:
# Program with comments
marks = 75
print("Marks:", marks)
ch4-structure.explanation: A well-structured program uses comments to explain the code and keeps statements neat and readable.

ch5-data-types.explanation: 10 is an integer (int). The type() function tells you the data type of a value.
A number with a decimal point is a float.
Text enclosed in quotes is a string (str).
True and False are boolean (bool) values used in conditions.
The same-looking value can have different types: 25 is int, 25.0 is float and "25" is str.

ch5-operators.code:
a = 9
b = 2
print(a + b)
print(a - b)
print(a * b)
print(a / b)
ch5-operators.explanation: The arithmetic operators +, -, * and / perform addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

ch5-operators.code:
a = 9
b = 2
print(a // b)
print(a % b)
print(a ** b)
ch5-operators.explanation: // gives the quotient without remainder, % gives the remainder, and ** raises to a power.
Relational operators compare two values and always give a boolean (True or False) result.

ch5-operators.code:
print(True and False)
print(True or False)
print(not True)
ch5-operators.explanation: Logical operators and, or and not combine boolean values.
Augmented assignment operators like += and *= update a variable using its current value.
Multiplication has higher precedence than addition; brackets change the order of evaluation.

ch5-type-conversion.explanation: int() converts a string of digits into an integer.
float() converts a string into a decimal number.

ch5-type-conversion.code:
n = 100
s = str(n)
print(s + " is a string now")
print(type(s))
ch5-type-conversion.explanation: str() converts a number into a string so that it can be joined with other text.
int() cuts off the decimal part, True becomes 1, and float() turns an integer into a decimal.

ch5-expressions.explanation: An expression is evaluated following operator precedence: * is done before +.
Brackets force the addition to be done before the multiplication.
This expression combines two comparisons with and; both are True so the result is True.
The expression uses powers and addition to compute 16 + 9.
The remainder (20 % 6) and the quotient (20 // 6) are computed first, then added.

ch6-control-structures.explanation: A sequence runs statements one after another with no decision or repetition.
Selection uses a condition to decide whether a block of code should run.

ch6-control-structures.code:
for i in range(3):
    print("Repeat", i)
ch6-control-structures.explanation: Iteration repeats a block of code a number of times using a loop.

ch6-sequence.explanation: In a sequence, statements execute in exactly the order in which they are written.

ch6-sequence.code:
length = 5
breadth = 3
area = length * breadth
print("Area =", area)
ch6-sequence.explanation: The values are computed step by step and the final result is displayed.

ch6-selection.explanation: A simple if runs its block only when the condition is True.
if-else chooses between two blocks: one when the condition is True and the other when it is False.
if-elif-else checks several conditions in order and runs the first block whose condition is True.
An if statement can be placed inside another if. This is called nesting.
The marks are read from the user and converted to an integer, then compared with the passing mark.

ch6-selection.code:
age = 25
has_id = True
if age >= 18 and has_id:
    print("Entry allowed")
ch6-selection.explanation: The and operator lets a condition depend on two things being true at the same time.

ch6-iteration.explanation: range(5) produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The loop body runs once for each value.
range(1, 6) produces numbers from 1 up to but not including 6.
The third value in range() is the step, so this prints even numbers from 2 to 10.

ch6-iteration.code:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
ch6-iteration.explanation: A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays True. The counter must be updated to stop it.

ch6-iteration.code:
n = 5
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total = total + i
print("Sum =", total)
ch6-iteration.explanation: This loop adds the numbers 1 to 5 into total using an accumulator variable.
break stops the loop completely as soon as the condition becomes true.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.
A loop inside another loop is a nested loop; the inner loop finishes fully for each outer value.

ch6-programs.code:
n = int(input("Enter n: "))
total = 0
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    total = total + i
print("Sum =", total)
ch6-programs.explanation: Reads n from the user and adds all numbers from 1 to n.

ch6-programs.code:
n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
fact = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    fact = fact * i
print("Factorial =", fact)
ch6-programs.explanation: Computes the factorial of n by multiplying the numbers 1 to n.
Prints the multiplication table of n from 1 to 10.

ch6-programs.output:
Enter first: 10
Enter second: 25
Enter third: 17
Largest is 25
ch6-programs.explanation: Reads three numbers and finds the largest using nested conditions.

ch6-programs.code:
n = int(input("How many numbers? "))
even = 0
for i in range(n):
    x = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    if x % 2 == 0:
        even = even + 1
print("Even count =", even)
ch6-programs.output:
How many numbers? 4
Enter a number: 2
Enter a number: 7
Enter a number: 8
Enter a number: 5
Even count = 2
ch6-programs.explanation: Reads n numbers and counts how many of them are even.

ch6-programs.code:
n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
rev = 0
while n > 0:
    rev = rev * 10 + n % 10
    n = n // 10
print("Reversed =", rev)
ch6-programs.explanation: Reverses the digits of a number using a while loop and the % and // operators.

ch7-error-messages.code:
# print(marks) before marks is defined
print("NameError: name 'marks' is not defined")
ch7-error-messages.explanation: A NameError appears when you use a variable that has not been defined yet.
A ZeroDivisionError appears when a number is divided by zero.

ch7-error-messages.code:
# print(int("abc"))
print("ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'")
ch7-error-messages.output: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
ch7-error-messages.explanation: A ValueError appears when a value cannot be converted to the requested type.
A SyntaxError appears when the code does not follow Python's rules, such as a missing colon.

ch7-exceptions.code:
# 10 / 0 causes this
print("ZeroDivisionError: division by zero")
ch7-exceptions.explanation: An exception is an error that stops the program while it is running.

ch7-exceptions.code:
# int("hello") causes this
print("ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'")
ch7-exceptions.output: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'
ch7-exceptions.explanation: ValueError is raised when the type is right but the value cannot be converted.

ch7-exceptions.code:
# numbers[5] on a 3-item list causes this
print("IndexError: list index out of range")
ch7-exceptions.output: IndexError: list index out of range
ch7-exceptions.explanation: IndexError is raised when you ask for an index that does not exist in a list.

ch7-exceptions.code:
# "5" + 5 causes this
print("TypeError: can only concatenate str (not \"int\") to str")
ch7-exceptions.output: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
ch7-exceptions.explanation: TypeError is raised when an operation is applied to the wrong type of value.

ch7-exceptions.code:
# printing an undefined variable causes this
print("NameError: name 'total' is not defined")
ch7-exceptions.explanation: NameError is raised when the program uses a name that has not been defined.

ch7-builtin-exceptions.code:
# print(score) where score was never assigned
print("NameError: name 'score' is not defined")
ch7-builtin-exceptions.explanation: NameError is a built-in exception raised for an undefined variable.

ch7-builtin-exceptions.code:
# 5 + "five" causes this
print("TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'")
ch7-builtin-exceptions.output: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
ch7-builtin-exceptions.explanation: TypeError is a built-in exception raised for incompatible data types.

ch7-builtin-exceptions.code:
# int("3.5a") causes this
print("ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5a'")
ch7-builtin-exceptions.output: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5a'
ch7-builtin-exceptions.explanation: ValueError is a built-in exception raised when a conversion fails.

ch7-builtin-exceptions.code:
# 8 % 0 causes this
print("ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero")
ch7-builtin-exceptions.output: ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero
ch7-builtin-exceptions.explanation: ZeroDivisionError is a built-in exception raised for division or modulo by zero.

ch7-builtin-exceptions.code:
# fruits[9] on a 2-item list causes this
print("IndexError: list index out of range")
ch7-builtin-exceptions.output: IndexError: list index out of range
ch7-builtin-exceptions.explanation: IndexError is a built-in exception raised for an invalid list index.

ch8-creating-lists.explanation: A list is created by writing values separated by commas inside square brackets.
A list can hold values of different data types in the same list.
The * operator can repeat a list, so [0] * 5 creates a list of five zeros.

ch8-accessing.explanation: List indexing starts at 0, so fruits[0] gives the first element.
fruits[2] gives the third element of the list.
A negative index counts from the end, so -1 gives the last element.
A slice [1:4] gives the elements from index 1 up to but not including index 4.
The step value 2 in a slice picks every second element of the list.

ch8-traversing.explanation: A for loop can go through a list directly, taking one element at a time.
Using range(len(list)) gives both the index and, through it, the element.

ch8-traversing.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
i = 0
while i < len(numbers):
    print(numbers[i])
    i = i + 1
ch8-traversing.explanation: A while loop can traverse a list by using an index that increases each time.

ch8-traversing.code:
numbers = [5, 10, 15]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total = total + n
print("Sum =", total)
ch8-traversing.explanation: Traversing a list with a loop makes it easy to add up all its elements.
The loop compares each element with the current largest and updates it when needed.

ch8-operators.explanation: The + operator joins two lists into a single new list.
The * operator repeats a list a given number of times.

ch8-operators.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
print("apple" in fruits)
print("mango" in fruits)
ch8-operators.explanation: The in operator checks whether an element is present in a list and gives True or False.
The == operator compares two lists element by element, including their order.

ch8-operations.explanation: append() adds a new element at the end of the list.
insert() adds an element at a given position, pushing the rest to the right.
remove() deletes the first occurrence of the given value from the list.
pop() removes and returns the last element of the list.
sort() arranges the elements of the list in ascending order.
reverse() changes the order of the elements so that the list is reversed.

ch8-builtin-functions.explanation: len() returns the number of elements in a list.
max() returns the largest element in a list.
min() returns the smallest element in a list.
sum() returns the total of all the numbers in a list.
sorted() returns a new list with the elements arranged in ascending order.

ch8-programs.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]
total = 0
for n in numbers:
    total = total + n
print("Sum =", total)
print("Average =", total / len(numbers))
ch8-programs.explanation: Finds the sum of all list elements and then divides it by the count to get the average.
Finds the largest element in a list by comparing each element with the current largest.
Counts how many elements in the list are even numbers.

ch8-programs.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
rev = []
for i in range(len(numbers) - 1, -1, -1):
    rev = rev + [numbers[i]]
print(rev)
ch8-programs.explanation: Builds a reversed copy of the list by reading it from the last index back to the first.

ch8-programs.code:
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
key = 20
found = False
for n in numbers:
    if n == key:
        found = True
print("Found:", found)
ch8-programs.explanation: Searches for a value in the list and reports whether it was found.
Finds the second largest element by tracking both the largest and the runner-up.
